positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/o: God, like the divine craftsman of Plato’s Timaeus, shaped an eternal, formless matter into an ordered cosmos rather than creating matter itself.
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/c: Matter is eternal and uncreated, though formless.
God is good and orders chaos into cosmos.
Evil derives from the recalcitrance of matter, not from God.
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/k: Wisdom of Solomon 11:17 (“out of formless matter”)
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/o: Plato’s Timaeus (c.360 BC) and Middle Platonism; adopted in some form by Hellenistic Jewish and early Christian writers (Justin may have assumed it, First Apology 10); defended explicitly by Hermogenes of Carthage (c.200) and refuted by Tertullian.
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/p: Modern: some process and open theists, Latter-day Saint cosmology
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/s: It explains evil without making God its author: disorder is rooted in matter’s resistance.
Genesis 1:2 (“without form and void”) and Wisdom 11:17 seem to presuppose pre-existing chaos.
It was the best philosophy of its age, and early Christian writers used it without sensing a conflict with Scripture.
Irenaeus, Theophilus and Tertullian object that an eternal matter would be a second god, equal to God in eternity.
If matter is the source of evil, salvation tends toward escape from the body rather than resurrection.
Biblical texts present God as the source of all things (John 1:3; Romans 11:36; Colossians 1:16).
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/r: Modern defenders (e.g. process theologians, some biblical scholars) answer that “chaos” in Genesis is not a rival god but the raw potential God persuades, and that ex nihilo is a philosophical import.
Latter-day Saints answer that eternal matter limits God’s responsibility for evil and fits Joseph Smith’s revelation.
positions/preexistent-matter-platonism/c: Its rejection by second-century theologians made creatio ex nihilo the Christian consensus.
Revived in modified form in process and Latter-day Saint thought.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/oneLine: The material world was made not by the highest God but by an ignorant or malevolent lesser power (the demiurge), so salvation is the escape of divine sparks from matter through secret knowledge (gnosis).
positions/gnostic-demiurge/coreClaims/0: The supreme God is utterly transcendent and did not make the material world.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/coreClaims/1: The creator of Genesis is a lesser, ignorant being (often identified with the God of Israel).
positions/gnostic-demiurge/coreClaims/2: Some human beings carry a divine spark trapped in matter.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/coreClaims/3: Salvation is liberation through knowledge, not resurrection of the body.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/origin: Second-century teachers such as Basilides (Alexandria, c.130), Valentinus (Rome, c.140) and Sethian texts later found at Nag Hammadi (1945); Marcion held a related distinction between the just Creator and the good Father.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/strongestArgu: It takes the reality of evil and suffering with great seriousness: a world this broken cannot be the direct work of the highest good.
It explains the felt alienation of the soul from the world and body.
It offered an esoteric, intellectually prestigious reading of Christianity for educated Romans.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/strongestObje: Irenaeus objects that it splits the one God and denies the goodness of creation, the incarnation and the resurrection of the flesh.
It makes salvation elitist, available only to the spiritual few.
Its readings of Genesis invert the plain sense and depend on secret traditions rather than public apostolic teaching.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/responses/0: Modern sympathisers argue that the Nag Hammadi texts reveal a diverse early Christianity unfairly suppressed, and that their critique of oppressive “archons” has moral force.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/responses/1: Scholars such as Karen King caution that “Gnosticism” is a later umbrella category and the groups differed widely.
positions/gnostic-demiurge/consequences/: Provoked Irenaeus’ Against Heresies and the “rule of faith” beginning “one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth”.
Lived on in Manichaeism, Paulicians, Bogomils and Cathars.
positions/augustinian-instantaneous-crea: Simultaneous creation with seminal reasons (Augustine)
instantaneous creation
rationes seminales
Augustine’s non-literal days

God created all things at once, in a single instant with time itself, implanting “seminal reasons” that unfold over time; the six days are a teaching device describing an order of knowledge, not 144 hours.
Creation was simultaneous (Sirach 18:1, Old Latin: “he created all things together”).
Living kinds were created potentially, as seeds or causal reasons that later develop.
The days are not solar days, since the sun appears only on day four.
Scripture should not be read so as to contradict what is known with certainty about nature.
Sirach 18:1
Genesis 1:1-2:4
Genesis 2:4-5
Psalm 33:9
Developed in Augustine’s Literal Meaning of Genesis (401-415) and City of God XI; anticipated by Philo and Origen’s non-literal readings.
Philo of Alexandria
Bonaventure (seminal reasons)
Modern: some evolutionary creationists and framework theorists invoke Augustine
It honours God’s transcendence: an omnipotent God needs no time to create.
It takes the text’s literary features seriously (light before the sun; two creation accounts).
It provides a classical precedent for reading Genesis in harmony with natural knowledge.
Young-earth creationists object that Augustine still believed in a young earth (under 6,000 years, City of God XII.10) and should not be enlisted for evolution.
Others note that his reading relied on a mistranslation of Sirach 18:1 in the Old Latin.
Aquinas and many later Western theologians preferred to treat the days as successive.
Defenders agree Augustine held a young earth but stress his principle — read Genesis without forcing it to contradict secure natural knowledge — rather than his conclusions.
Augustine himself offered his reading tentatively and allowed other interpretations.
Kept non-literal readings of the days respectable in the West.
Cited by Galileo (1615) and by 19th- and 20th-century harmonisers.
positions/young-earth-creationism/oneLin: God created the universe in six ordinary days roughly 6,000-10,000 years ago; animal death and natural evil followed Adam’s fall; Noah’s global Flood laid down most of the fossil record.
positions/young-earth-creationism/coreCl: The genealogies give a recent date for creation.
There was no animal death before the fall (Romans 5:12; 8:20-22).
Mainstream geology and evolutionary biology rest on naturalistic assumptions and can be reinterpreted.
Jesus and Paul treated Adam and the Flood as historical.
positions/young-earth-creationism/origin: The plain-reading young earth was the common pre-modern view (e.g. Ussher’s 4004 BC, 1650), but modern YEC took shape through the Adventist George McCready Price’s flood geology (1923) and Whitcomb and Morris’s The Genesis Flood (1961).
positions/young-earth-creationism/strong: It reads Genesis as Jesus and the apostles appear to have read it, and as most Christians did before the 18th century.
It protects the link between Adam’s sin, death and redemption: death is an enemy, not God’s creative tool.
Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath week in a literal creation week.
It refuses to let shifting scientific consensus become the arbiter of Scripture.
Geologists, physicists and biologists, including many Christians, object that multiple independent dating methods and starlight distances show an ancient universe and earth.

Old-earth evangelicals note that Genesis 1 itself contains non-literal signals (days before the sun; the open-ended seventh day) and that conservatives like Warfield and the authors of The Fundamentals accepted an old earth.
Critics argue that insisting on YEC as a test of orthodoxy creates needless barriers to faith and drives scientists away.
positions/young-earth-creationism/respon: YEC scientists (e.g. at ICR, AiG, the Creation Research Society) propose alternative models (accelerated decay, white-hole cosmology, catastrophic plate tectonics).
They argue that “appearance of age” is inherent in any mature creation (Adam was created adult).
They answer that the authority of Scripture, not of fallible science, must decide.
positions/young-earth-creationism/conseq: Became majority view among U.S. evangelicals in the late 20th century and spread globally (Korea, Brazil, Nigeria, Kenya, Turkey’s Islamic creationism borrowed from it).
Created museums, curricula and legal campaigns; contributed to evangelical distrust of mainstream science.
positions/old-earth-day-age/oneLine: The “days” of Genesis are long ages, and God created in stages over billions of years, directly creating new kinds (including humans) at intervals; Scripture and nature, read rightly, agree.
positions/old-earth-day-age/coreClaims/0: The Hebrew yom can mean an indefinite period (Genesis 2:4).
positions/old-earth-day-age/coreClaims/2: The order of the days broadly matches the scientific record.
positions/old-earth-day-age/coreClaims/3: God intervened directly to create life, major kinds and humanity; Adam and Eve were historical.
positions/old-earth-day-age/origin: Proposed by 19th-century harmonisers such as Hugh Miller (Testimony of the Rocks, 1857) and Arnold Guyot; held by William Jennings Bryan at the Scopes trial; popularised today by Hugh Ross’s Reasons to Believe (1986).
positions/old-earth-day-age/strongestArg: It respects both the authority of Genesis and the overwhelming evidence for an old universe.
It retains a historical Adam and special creation, protecting human uniqueness.
It uses the Bible’s own flexible use of “day” and the unending seventh day.
positions/old-earth-day-age/strongestObj: Young-earth creationists object that “evening and morning” and numbered days signal ordinary days and that the view admits death before the fall.
Scientists and evolutionary creationists object that the fossil and genetic evidence shows common descent, not repeated special creations.
Literary interpreters object that the order of Genesis 1 does not actually match science (e.g. birds before land animals; vegetation before the sun).
positions/old-earth-day-age/responses/0: Day-age advocates answer that animal death is not the “death” Paul ties to sin (Romans 5 concerns human death).
positions/old-earth-day-age/responses/1: They argue that progressive creation explains sudden appearances in the fossil record (e.g. the Cambrian) better than gradualism.
positions/old-earth-day-age/consequences: Allowed many conservative Protestants (including the authors of The Fundamentals) to accept geology without evolution.
Lost ground to YEC after 1961 but revived through Reasons to Believe.
positions/gap-theory/oneLine: Between Genesis 1:1 (an original creation) and 1:2 (“the earth became without form and void”) lies an indefinite gap, often linked with Lucifer’s fall; the six days describe a recent re-creation.
positions/gap-theory/coreClaims/0: Genesis 1:2 should be translated “became” waste and void, signalling a judgement.
positions/gap-theory/coreClaims/1: The geological ages and fossils belong to the pre-Adamic world.
positions/gap-theory/coreClaims/2: The six days are literal days of restoration.
positions/gap-theory/coreClaims/3: Isaiah 14, Ezekiel 28 and Jeremiah 4:23-26 hint at a primeval catastrophe tied to Satan’s rebellion.
positions/gap-theory/origin: Popularised by Thomas Chalmers from about 1814; spread by G. H. Pember’s Earth’s Earliest Ages (1876) and the Scofield Reference Bible notes (1909), and widely held in early 20th-century fundamentalism and Pentecostalism.
positions/gap-theory/strongestArguments/: It allows a literal six-day week and an old earth at once.
It offers a setting for the fall of the angels before Eden.
It was endorsed by trusted reference works and preachers of the dispensationalist movement.
positions/gap-theory/strongestObjections: Hebrew grammarians object that the waw-disjunctive in Genesis 1:2 describes a state (“the earth was”), not a change (“became”).
Young-earth creationists reject it for allowing death before Adam; geologists find no break between a “pre-Adamic” and present world.
Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 are, in context, oracles against the kings of Babylon and Tyre.
positions/gap-theory/responses/0: Gap theorists answer that hayah can mean “became” (as in Genesis 19:26) and that the prophetic texts point beyond their human subjects.
positions/gap-theory/responses/1: They argue that the theory is a modest harmonisation, not a dogma.
positions/gap-theory/consequences/0: Dominated fundamentalist teaching before 1960 through the Scofield Bible.
positions/gap-theory/consequences/1: Largely displaced by young-earth creationism after The Genesis Flood.
